content: Centella asiatica is a small, herbaceous annual plant belonging to the Apiaceae family, which also includes carrots and dill. It is native to regions such as northern Australia, New Guinea, Melanesia, Malaysia, Iran, and other parts of Asia. Commonly referred to as Gotu Kola, Asiatic Pennywort, Luei Gong Gen, Antanan, Pegaga, Kula Kud, and Brahmi (though the latter name is also used for Bacopa monnieri and other herbs), this plant has been widely used in Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine. Its botanical synonyms include Hydrocotyle asiatica L. and Trisanthus cochinchinensis (Lour). Stem Characteristics The plant features slender, creeping stolons that are green to reddish-green in color, which interconnect individual plants. Its leaves are long-stalked, green, and kidney-shaped (reniform) with rounded apices. The leaves have a smooth texture and display palmately netted veins. They are attached to pericladial petioles, which are approximately 20 cm in length. The rootstock consists of vertically growing rhizomes that are cream-colored and covered with root hairs. Flower Characteristics The flowers of Centella asiatica are pinkish to red and grow in small, rounded clusters (umbels) near the soil surface. Each flower is partially enclosed by two green bracts. These hermaphroditic flowers are minute, measuring less than 3 mm in size, and have 5-6 corolla lobes. Each flower contains five stamens and two styles. The fruit of the plant is densely reticulate, which differentiates it from species of Hydrocotyle that have smooth, ribbed, or warty fruit. The plant matures within three months, and the entire plant, including its roots, is harvested manually. Habitat Centella asiatica thrives in wet, low-lying areas such as ditches. In regions like India and Southeast Asia, the plant is often subject to bacterial contamination, likely due to being harvested from sewage ditches. As an aquatic plant, it is highly sensitive to water pollutants, which can easily be absorbed into its tissues. Culinary Uses In Sri Lankan cuisine, Centella asiatica is used as a leafy green, most commonly prepared as mallung, a traditional side dish served with rice and curry. It pairs particularly well with vegetarian dishes such as lentil curry (parippu), jackfruit curry, or pumpkin curry. Mallung typically includes finely chopped Gotu Kola leaves, grated coconut, and may also feature ingredients like chilies, lime or lemon juice, dried fish, curry leaves, and spices such as fried mustard seeds. Additionally, Centella leaves are used to make a sweet beverage known as pennywort drink. Pharmacology and Active Constituents Centella asiatica contains several bioactive compounds, including: Bacoside A: Facilitates the release of nitric oxide, promoting relaxation of the aorta and veins, thereby improving blood flow. Bacoside B: A protein that nourishes brain cells. Asiaticosides: Stimulate the reticuloendothelial system, which is involved in blood cell formation, iron metabolism, immune responses, and inflammation. Asiaticosides also enhance connective tissue development, keratinization, and the healing of ulcers, skin injuries, and connective tissue damage. They reduce capillary fragility and promote the synthesis of lipids and proteins essential for healthy skin. Other notable constituents include: Minerals: Calcium, Iron, Selenium, Magnesium Vitamins: Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C), Beta Carotene Essential oils: Camphor Triterpenes: Betulic Acid, Brahmic Acid, Isobrahmic Acid, Thankunic Acid Saponins: Brahmoside, Thankuniside, Asiaticoside A & B, Brahminoside, Madecassoside Flavones: Quercetin Medicinal Actions Centella asiatica exhibits a range of pharmacological properties, including: Mild adaptogenic effects Antibacterial and antiviral activity Anti-inflammatory and anti-ulcerogenic properties Anxiolytic effects Cerebral tonic and circulatory stimulant actions Diuretic, nervine, and vulnerary (wound-healing) properties Medicinal Uses and Research When consumed raw as a salad leaf, Centella asiatica is believed to promote youthfulness. In Thailand, it is consumed as a refreshing afternoon beverage. A decoction of its leaves is thought to alleviate hypertension and serve as a general health tonic. The leaves are also applied as a poultice to treat open sores. Chewing the plant for extended periods has been reported to induce meditative states, though this practice is considered risky due to potential temporomandibular joint pain. In 1979, Richard Lucas claimed that a subspecies called Hydrocotyle asiatica minor (allegedly from Sri Lanka and referred to as Fo ti tieng) contained a longevity factor called Vitamin X, which was said to benefit the brain and endocrine glands. However, no scientific evidence supports the existence of this subspecies or Vitamin X. Despite this, Centella asiatica has demonstrated credible effects on cerebral circulation and dermatological health. Scientific studies have confirmed the plant's ability to aid wound healing, which underpins its traditional use in treating leprosy. Treatment with Centella asiatica stimulates scar maturation through the production of type I collagen, reduces inflammatory reactions, and decreases myofibroblast production. Steroids isolated from the plant have been used in leprosy treatment. Preliminary evidence also suggests that Centella asiatica may have nootropic effects, enhancing brain function, attention span, and concentration. Additionally, it possesses antioxidant properties, supports venous insufficiency, and is used in Thailand for opium detoxification. Folklore Centella asiatica features in the longevity myth of Tai Chi Chuan master Li Ching-Yun, who reportedly lived to be 256 years old, partly due to his use of traditional Chinese herbs, including Gotu Kola. A Sri Lankan folklore tale recounts the story of a 10th-century king named Aruna, who claimed that Gotu Kola provided him with the energy and stamina to satisfy his 50-woman harem.
